planting.note: Direct sow in spring where runoff collects, in dappled shade along a stream bank or in full sun at a pond edge; cold-moist stratification improves uniformity.

directions: The most widespread Glyceria in North America, this grass is tolerant of both shaded woodland seeps and open sunny marsh edges, making it one of the few truly shade-tolerant wet-soil grasses for rain gardens and pond margins. Plant it where runoff collects, since it resents drying out between waterings. Its airy, nodding panicles turn a soft straw color by late summer and persist well into winter, offering structure after summer wildflowers fade.

planting.note: Direct sow with cold-moist stratification into a bog garden, rain garden low point, or pond margin where the crown stays consistently wet to saturated.

directions: Showy, inflated, pendulous spikelets give this species its namesake 'rattlesnake' seed heads and strong textural interest unlike any ornamental grass already in common cultivation. It is a true obligate-wetland grass that will sulk or die out in anything short of consistently wet to saturated soil, so it is not a general-purpose ornamental grass. The inflated, bead-like spikelets dangling from wiry branches show best when the plant is backlit by low sun.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or stratify ~60 days into humus-rich soil on rocky slopes or streambank terraces under high-canopy trees.

directions: A genuinely shade-tolerant member of a genus otherwise represented almost entirely by full-sun ornamental cultivars, this grass occupies the same forest-floor niche as woodland sedges but offers finer, grassier texture and airy late-season seed panicles that catch low autumn light under deciduous canopy. It spreads slowly by short rhizomes, forming loose colonies rather than tight clumps, so give it room among ferns and woodland wildflowers rather than isolating it as a specimen. Avoid heavy mulch that smothers the shallow rhizomes.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or stratify ~60 days into thin, rocky soil on a slope or ledge with excellent drainage; soggy winter soil is more likely to kill it than drought.

directions: This grass is built for exactly the site gardeners struggle with most: dry shade over rock or thin, rocky soil on slopes and ledges, where almost nothing else in the genus will grow. It forms sparse, wiry clumps rather than a dense sward, making its understated habit best used as a filler among larger dry-shade perennials rather than a focal grass. Excellent drainage is essential — its real value is persisting where turf and most ornamentals fail entirely.

planting.note: Divide rhizomes or direct sow in spring under trees with consistent soil moisture; site away from paths since leaf margins carry minute serrations.

directions: One of the few native grasses that actually prefers shade over sun, this species naturally colonizes the understory of moist riparian forests, where it forms loose, sprawling mats more shade-tolerant than its wetter relative Leersia oryzoides. It self-sows and spreads by rhizomes to form an informal groundcover under trees with consistent soil moisture, but is not aggressive enough to be a nuisance in a typical garden bed. Leaf margins carry minute serrations, so site it away from paths where bare skin brushes the foliage.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall at the base of a boulder or along a shaded woodland path edge on rocky, well-drained soil; this cool-season grower goes semi-dormant in summer heat.

directions: This diminutive, delicate wedgescale is sized for small-scale plantings — a shaded rock garden, the base of a boulder, or a woodland path edge — rather than mass plantings where larger ornamental grasses would overwhelm it. It pushes new growth in fall and early spring and goes semi-dormant in summer heat, so pair it with later-emerging companions that can take over seasonal interest. Good drainage on a rocky or ledge-like site mimics its native habitat and prevents crown rot in wet winters.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into a rain garden or mesic meadow planting; rely on vigorous self-seeding rather than expecting individual plants to persist for many years.

directions: This adaptable short-lived native bunchgrass is unusually tolerant of a wide range of soil moisture, naturally occupying pasture edges, pond margins, and open woods alike, filling gaps in rain gardens or mesic meadow plantings without demanding a precise moisture regime. It serves as a host plant for the white-lined sphinx moth, adding wildlife value to a naturalistic planting. Its oat-like seed heads age from pale green to tan with occasional purple blush, giving good seasonal color change.

planting.note: Direct sow fall with cold-moist stratification into mesic, well-drained, calcium-rich forest soil in dappled to full shade; avoid acidic or poorly drained sites.

directions: A true deep-shade woodland grass of calcareous rocky forests, this species carries distinctive glossy black-brown seeds held in loose, open panicles and an upright habit that is nearly leafless at the base, giving it a very different silhouette from typical shade sedges and grasses. It will not thrive in acidic or poorly drained sites, so give it rocky, calcium-rich forest soil instead. Its dark seeds contrast well against the lighter foliage of ferns and sedges in a shaded rock garden; confirm supplier listings under the synonyms Oryzopsis racemosa or Patis racemosa if this name turns up no results.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into dry, sandy, acidic soil along a woodland margin or lean meadow; leave undivided for several years once established, since it resents root disturbance.

directions: Named for the fine silvery pubescence on its leaf sheaths, this grass has a soft, frosted look distinct from the coarser danthonias already in cultivation, thriving in the dry, sandy, acidic soils of southeastern coastal-plain and Piedmont pine-oak woodlands. It does best left undivided for several years, since it resents root disturbance once established. Use it along woodland margins or in a sandy, lean meadow planting where its low, tidy basal foliage persists as winter interest after the seed stalks shatter.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into a woodland rain garden edge or shaded slope that collects runoff; tolerates full sun to deep shade as long as soil stays reliably moist.

directions: Unlike the mostly full-sun ornamental cultivars of its better-known relative Deschampsia cespitosa, this West Coast native tolerates the full range from open sun to deep shade as long as soil stays reliably moist, making it a flexible choice for a woodland rain garden edge or a shaded slope. Its arching stems emerge yellowish-green in spring and mature to soft gold by summer, giving good seasonal color shift without staking or division. Being deer-resistant and modestly self-sowing, it works well massed as a living mulch beneath shrubs in consistently damp Pacific slope gardens.
